topic: Advanced Collocations for Discussion and Writing

scenarios.context: Two classmates prepare for a class debate on banning cars from the city centre.

speakerA.en: Let's start by putting forward our main argument. I'd say the strongest point is that cars cause serious air pollution.
Good point. Let's weigh up the pros and cons before we decide how to present our case.
We should bear in mind that some cities have already done this successfully. Do you remember the example from the article?
Then we can draw the conclusion that the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, as long as public transport improves.
Right. Shall we divide the work, with you covering the economic side and me the environmental side?
And let's rehearse our rebuttals, so we can respond quickly when the other side attacks our position.

speakerB.en: Agreed, but we also need to take into account the shopkeepers who depend on drivers. Otherwise, the other team will raise concerns we haven't answered.
On the plus side, a ban would reduce noise, improve safety and encourage people to walk. On the downside, it could hurt local businesses.
Yes, shops there reported that sales rose once the streets became more pleasant. That could help us make a strong case.
Precisely. We can't just ban cars and hope for the best; we have to provide a realistic alternative.
Fine by me. I'll look for hard evidence, because a vague claim won't carry much weight.
Good plan. If we prepare thoroughly, we should have a real chance of winning the argument.

scenarios.context: A teacher gives a student feedback on a draft essay about online learning.

speakerA.en: Your introduction is clear, but you need to state your position more firmly. Right now, it reads like a neutral summary.
Balance is important, but you still have to make a point. A strong essay strikes a balance between both views and a clear opinion.
Both help. Back up each claim with evidence, and always explain why it matters instead of simply quoting figures.
Not yet. It's a general statement. Draw attention to a specific group, such as parents working full time, and give a concrete example.
Avoid that. Sum up your main arguments in fresh words, and end with a thought that leaves a lasting impression.
It's essential. Acknowledging a counter-argument and then refuting it shows maturity and makes your case far more persuasive.

speakerB.en: I wasn't sure whether to take a side. I thought a balanced view would look more academic.
I see. Should I support my claims with statistics, or are examples enough?
That makes sense. In my second paragraph, I wrote that online learning is more flexible. Is that a convincing case?
Got it. What about the conclusion? I tend to repeat what I've already said.
Is it acceptable to mention an opposing view that I disagree with?
Thank you. I'll revise the draft and submit it again on Monday.

scenarios.context: A start-up founder and an investor discuss the company's progress.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting me. Your product has attracted a lot of attention, but can you make a profit?
What gives you a competitive edge over larger firms?
That's impressive, but I notice you're working on a tight budget. Is that sustainable?
Have you considered hiring more staff?
Sounds ambitious. What's the biggest risk?
I'll discuss it with my partners and get back to you by the end of the week.

speakerB.en: Not yet, but we're on track to break even by the end of the year. Sales have been rising steadily.
We respond to customers more quickly, and our prices are lower because we run a very lean operation.
For now, yes. The heavy workload is a challenge, though, and the team is struggling to meet deadlines.
We'd love to, but we need a steady income first. That's why we hope to secure funding this month to launch a major advertising campaign.
A sudden drop in demand, honestly. But we've built up a loyal customer base, which should help us ride out any difficulties.
Thank you. We'll be waiting for your answer.

scenarios.context: Two volunteers plan a campaign about plastic waste in their town.

speakerA.en: Plastic waste is a growing concern in our town. We need to raise awareness before the problem gets worse.
The council says it's doing its best to tackle the issue, but I haven't noticed any real change.
Do you think people will respond? Many of them seem indifferent.
What about shops? They could reduce packaging if there were enough demand.
In the foreseeable future, I'd like to see a ban on single-use bags.
Then let's organise a meeting next week and invite the mayor.

speakerB.en: I agree. If we don't take urgent action, it will pose a serious threat to the river and the wildlife.
Public opinion could force their hand. A widespread campaign with posters and social media might make them act.
Some will, and a small group of committed people can make a real difference. Change usually starts small.
Exactly. Once customers start to demand plastic-free products, businesses will have to meet that demand or lose them.
That's realistic. Several towns have already introduced one, and the results have been very encouraging.
Good plan. Let's draft the invitation tonight and get things moving.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss a film adaptation of their favourite novel.

speakerA.en: Did you see the film of our favourite novel? I was bitterly disappointed. They changed the ending completely.
True, but the pace was painfully slow in the middle. I nearly fell asleep.
It's widely believed that the book is untouchable, and I'm afraid I belong to that group.
Would you strongly recommend it to someone who hasn't read the book?
Maybe I'm being unfair. It's highly unlikely that any film could satisfy every reader.
I might. I'm deeply attached to the characters, so I admit I'm biased.

speakerB.en: I was deeply surprised too, but I wouldn't say it was a disaster. The acting was highly impressive.
Fair enough. Still, the director was fully aware that he couldn't fit everything in. Adaptations always involve difficult choices.
I can tell. There was a heated debate about it online, and some fans even signed a petition.
Actually, yes. Without the comparison, I think they'd enjoy it. It's a thoroughly entertaining story.
Exactly. Perhaps you should watch it again with an open mind and decide then.
That's perfectly understandable. Honestly, your passion for the book is what makes your opinion interesting.
